questions.stem: What does „die Gleichaltrigen“ mean?
options: The elderly, people of great age
Equals, people of the same rank
Peers, people of the same age
questions.explanation: „Gleich“ is 'same' and „alt“ is 'old', so „die Gleichaltrigen“ are people your own age. It is an adjectival noun, so it declines: „mit Gleichaltrigen“. Equality of rank would be „gleichberechtigt“.

questions.stem: What does „das Selbstbewusstsein“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Selbstbewusst“ is confident, aware of your own worth. English 'self-conscious', meaning shy or awkward, is „gehemmt“ or „unsicher“, so the look-alike reverses the meaning.

questions.stem: What does „das Vorbild“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Das Vorbild“ is someone you look up to: „Meine Tante ist mein Vorbild.“ A prejudice is „das Vorurteil“, which also starts with „vor-“.

questions.stem: What does „die Sucht“ mean, as in „die Handysucht“?
questions.explanation: „Die Sucht“ is addiction, so „die Handysucht“ is phone addiction. It looks like „suchen“, 'to search', but is a different word; a habit is „die Gewohnheit“.

questions.stem: What does „Ich mache mir Sorgen um meine Prüfungen“ mean?
options: I'm taking care of my exams
I'm making plans for my exams
questions.explanation: „Sich Sorgen machen um“ is 'to worry about'. Looking after something is „sich kümmern um“, which has the same preposition, so the two are easy to swap.

questions.stem: What does „Rechte und Pflichten“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Das Recht“ is a right and „die Pflicht“ a duty or obligation, so „die Schulpflicht“ is compulsory schooling. „Das Gesetz“ is a law.

questions.stem: In Germany, what does it mean to be „volljährig“?
options: To be old enough to work part-time
To have reached the age of 18
To be over the age of 65
questions.explanation: „Volljährig“, literally 'full of years', means legally adult, which in Germany is 18. Retirement age is „das Rentenalter“.

questions.stem: Read the post: „Ich bin in Melbourne geboren, aber meine Eltern kommen aus Österreich. Zu Hause sprechen wir Deutsch, und manchmal weiß ich nicht genau, wo ich hingehöre.“ What does the writer say?
options: She wants to move to Austria with her parents
She speaks German only when she is at school
She sometimes isn't sure where she belongs
She doesn't know where her parents come from
questions.explanation: „Wo ich hingehöre“ is 'where I belong', and „manchmal weiß ich nicht genau“ is 'sometimes I don't quite know'. Her parents' origin is stated clearly, and German is spoken „zu Hause“, not at school.

questions.stem: Read: „Seit ich das Handy abends aus dem Schlafzimmer verbanne, schlafe ich viel besser.“ What has the writer changed?
options: She goes to bed earlier than she used to
She has moved her bed into another room
She keeps her phone out of the bedroom at night
She has stopped using her phone altogether
questions.explanation: „Verbannen“ is to banish, and „abends aus dem Schlafzimmer“ says where and when. „Seit“ with the present tells you she still does it, and it is the phone that moves, not the bed.

questions.stem: Read: „Für mich zählt nicht, wie viel man verdient, sondern ob man etwas Sinnvolles tut.“ What matters to the writer?
options: Having a lot of free time
Being well known for one's work
questions.explanation: „Nicht …, sondern …“ rejects the first idea and replaces it with the second, so money matters less than „etwas Sinnvolles“, something meaningful. Reading only the first half gives the opposite answer.

questions.stem: What does „sich streiten“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Sich streiten“ is to argue or quarrel: „Ich streite mich oft mit meinem Bruder.“ Making up afterwards is „sich versöhnen“.

questions.stem: What does „Ich verstehe mich gut mit meiner Schwester“ mean?
options: I explain myself well to my sister
I agree with everything my sister says
I get on well with my sister
questions.explanation: Reflexive „sich verstehen mit“ means to get on with someone. Without „sich“, „ich verstehe meine Schwester“ would mean 'I understand my sister'.

questions.stem: What does „die Großfamilie“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Die Großfamilie“ includes grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins. Grandparents alone are „die Großeltern“, and the family tree is „der Stammbaum“.

questions.stem: What does „Erziehung“ mean in „Meine Eltern legen viel Wert auf eine strenge Erziehung“?
questions.explanation: „Die Erziehung“ is how parents raise a child, so „eine strenge Erziehung“ is a strict upbringing. Education in the sense of schooling and knowledge is „die Bildung“, which is the usual mistranslation.

questions.stem: What is „der Generationenkonflikt“?
options: Conflict between older and younger generations
A family dispute over an inheritance
questions.explanation: „Die Generation“ plus „der Konflikt“ gives conflict between generations, such as parents and teenagers. Rivalry between siblings is „die Geschwisterrivalität“.

questions.stem: Read: „Mein Opa wohnt seit dem Tod meiner Oma bei uns. Am Anfang war es eng, aber jetzt kocht er jeden Sonntag und erzählt Geschichten von früher.“ How has living together changed?
options: The grandmother now cooks every Sunday
It was cramped at first but is now enjoyable
It was enjoyable at first but is now cramped
The grandfather has now moved out again
questions.explanation: „Am Anfang war es eng“ is 'at first it was cramped', and „aber jetzt“ turns to the positives. „Seit dem Tod meiner Oma“ tells you the grandmother has died, so she cannot be the cook.

questions.stem: Read: „In unserer Straße kennt jeder jeden. Wenn jemand in Urlaub fährt, gießt die Nachbarin die Blumen.“ What does this suggest?
options: The neighbour sells flowers in the street
Nobody in the street goes on holiday
The neighbours know and help one another
The street is busy with tourists
questions.explanation: „Jeder kennt jeden“ is 'everyone knows everyone', and watering („gießen“) a neighbour's plants is a small favour. „In Urlaub fahren“ shows that people do go away.

questions.stem: What does „der Lebenslauf“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Der Lebenslauf“, literally 'course of life', is the CV sent with a job application. A fun run would be „der Volkslauf“.

questions.stem: What is „ein Vorstellungsgespräch“?
questions.explanation: „Sich vorstellen“ is to introduce yourself, and „das Gespräch“ is a conversation, so „das Vorstellungsgespräch“ is a job interview. A theatre show is „die Vorstellung“ alone.

questions.stem: What is „ein Praktikum“?
options: A practice exam before the real one
questions.explanation: „Ein Praktikum machen“ is to do work experience or an internship, often while at school or university. A practice exam is „die Probeprüfung“, and training is „das Training“.

questions.stem: What does „ehrenamtlich“ mean, as in „Sie arbeitet ehrenamtlich im Tierheim“?
options: As a manager, in charge of others
As a paid casual worker on weekends
questions.explanation: „Das Ehrenamt“ is unpaid work done for the community, so she volunteers at the animal shelter. Casual paid work is „der Nebenjob“ or „der Minijob“.

questions.stem: What does „sich bewerben um“ mean, as in „Ich bewerbe mich um eine Stelle als Koch“?
questions.explanation: „Sich bewerben um“ is to apply for a position, and „die Bewerbung“ is the application. „Die Stelle“ here means a job or position.

questions.stem: What is „das Gehalt“?
questions.explanation: „Das Gehalt“ is a regular salary; „der Lohn“ is usually hourly or weekly wages. A pension is „die Rente“ and a tax is „die Steuer“.

questions.stem: What does „eine Lehre machen“ mean?
options: To learn a lesson the hard way
questions.explanation: „Die Lehre“ here is a vocational apprenticeship, and the apprentice is „der Lehrling“ or „der/die Auszubildende“. A teacher is „der Lehrer“, which shares the root.

questions.stem: What is „das duale System“ of vocational training in Germany?
options: Study at two universities in two countries at once
A school that teaches both German and English
A choice between full-time and part-time study
Training split between a workplace and a vocational school
questions.explanation: Apprentices spend part of the week with an employer and part at a „Berufsschule“. It is why most German trade qualifications come with paid work experience built in.

questions.stem: What is „ein Freiwilliges Soziales Jahr“?
options: A gap year spent travelling overseas
A compulsory year of military service
A year of school spent on exchange abroad
A year of voluntary service in a social field
questions.explanation: Young people can spend a year volunteering, for example in a hospital or aged care, often between school and study. „Freiwillig“ is voluntary, which rules out compulsory service.

questions.stem: Read: „Nach dem Abitur möchte ich nicht sofort studieren. Ich will erst ein Jahr arbeiten, um herauszufinden, was mir wirklich liegt.“ Why does the writer want to work first?
options: Because the university is far away
To find out what really suits her
To earn money for her studies
Because she failed her final exams
questions.explanation: „Um … herauszufinden“ gives the purpose, 'to find out', and „was mir liegt“ is an idiom for what you are good at or suited to. Money and distance are never mentioned, and „nach dem Abitur“ shows she has finished school.

questions.stem: Read: „Meine Mutter arbeitet seit letztem Jahr nur noch vier Tage pro Woche. Sie verdient weniger, hat aber endlich Zeit für sich.“ What does the text say?
options: She earns more and works fewer hours
She lost her job last year
She now works seven days a week
She earns less but has more time for herself
questions.explanation: „Nur noch vier Tage“ means 'only four days now', and „verdient weniger“ is 'earns less'. „Aber endlich Zeit für sich“ gives the gain, a better work-life balance.

questions.stem: Read: „Ich habe die Schule mit 16 verlassen. Heute, mit 45, hole ich an der Abendschule das Abitur nach.“ Which idea from the theme does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: „Etwas nachholen“ is catching up on something missed, and doing it at „Abendschule“, night school, at 45 is lifelong learning. Nothing in the text involves another generation.

questions.stem: What does „Ich drücke dir die Daumen!“ mean?
options: I'll keep my fingers crossed for you!
I'll give you a thumbs up!
I'll put some pressure on you to do it!
questions.explanation: Germans 'press their thumbs' where English speakers cross their fingers, for exams or interviews. It is a fixed idiom that cannot be translated word for word.

questions.stem: What does „Ich habe die Nase voll“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Die Nase voll haben“ is to be sick of something: „Ich habe die Nase voll von den Hausaufgaben.“ Having had enough to eat is „Ich bin satt“.

questions.stem: What does „Das ist mir Wurst“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Das ist mir Wurst“ or „egal“ is indifference: 'it's all the same to me'. It is casual, so it suits a chat with a friend, not a conversation with a teacher.

questions.stem: Your friend says „Ich verstehe nur Bahnhof.“ What is the best reply?
questions.explanation: „Ich verstehe nur Bahnhof“ means 'it's all Greek to me', so offering to explain again keeps the exchange going. The replies about trains take the idiom literally.

questions.stem: In a conversation, which phrase asks someone to repeat what they said?
options: Könnten Sie bitte etwas lauter sprechen?
questions.explanation: „Wiederholen“ is to repeat. „Erklären“ asks for an explanation, which is a different request when you simply did not hear.

questions.stem: In a discussion, which phrase hands the turn to the other speaker?
questions.explanation: „Was meinst du dazu?“ asks for the other person's view, which invites them to speak. The others give your own opinion and keep the turn.

questions.stem: Which phrase disagrees politely?
options: Da muss ich dir völlig recht geben.
questions.explanation: „Anderer Meinung sein“ is to be of a different opinion, a polite way to disagree. The other three all agree, „genauso“ meaning 'exactly the same way'.

questions.stem: In a role-play you meet your exchange partner's grandmother for the first time. Which greeting suits?
options: „Hi Frau Weber, wie geht's dir denn so?“
„Tschüss, Frau Weber, bis zum nächsten Mal!“
„Guten Tag, Frau Weber. Freut mich, Sie kennenzulernen.“
questions.explanation: An older adult you have just met is addressed with „Sie“ and her surname. „Dich“ and „dir“ are the familiar forms, and „Tschüss“ closes a conversation rather than opening one.

questions.stem: Which phrase is a natural way to close a conversation with your host family's neighbour?
options: „Guten Tag! Wie geht es Ihnen heute?“
„Es war schön, mit Ihnen zu sprechen. Auf Wiedersehen!“
„Es war schön, mit dir zu sprechen. Mach's gut!“
questions.explanation: A neighbour you do not know well is „Sie“, and „Auf Wiedersehen“ is the polite farewell. „Mach's gut“ with „dir“ suits a friend, and the last two open a conversation.

questions.stem: Mid-sentence you realise you said „gestern“ instead of „morgen“. Which phrase corrects it smoothly?
questions.explanation: „Ich meine …“ introduces a self-correction, the way English uses 'I mean'. „Wie bitte?“ asks the other person to repeat, and the other two keep the mistake.

questions.stem: How do you begin a formal email to a company when you don't know who will read it?
questions.explanation: „Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren“ is the standard formal opening to an unknown reader. „Mit freundlichen Grüßen“ is the formal closing, not an opening.

questions.stem: How do you begin an informal letter to your friend Paul?
questions.explanation: „Lieb-“ takes adjective endings, and Paul is male, so „Lieber Paul“; a girl would be „Liebe Anna“. „Sehr geehrter“ is far too formal for a friend.

questions.stem: In a German letter, how does the text after „Liebe Anna,“ begin on the next line?
options: With a lower-case letter, unless the word is a noun
With a capital letter, as after a full stop
With an exclamation mark, then a capital
With the date and the writer's address
questions.explanation: The comma means the greeting and the first line form one sentence, so the next word is lower case: „vielen Dank für deinen Brief“. Nouns and the formal „Sie“ keep their capitals.

questions.stem: What does „LG“ stand for at the end of a text message to a friend?
questions.explanation: „LG“ is the abbreviated „Liebe Grüße“, 'kind regards', for informal messages. In a formal email it would be written out as „Mit freundlichen Grüßen“.
